retired.text:
The eight presumptive signs of death are:

{{c1::Unresponsiveness to painful stimuli}}

{{c1::Lack of a carotid pulse or heartbeat}}

{{c1::Absence of chest rise and fall}}

{{c1::No deep tendon or corneal reflexes}}

{{c1::Absence of pupillary reactivity}}

{{c1::No systolic blood pressure}}

{{c1::Profound cyanosis}}

{{c1::Lowered or decreased body temperature}}
retired.back_extra:
Distinguish: presumptive signs only suggest death, whereas definitive (conclusive) signs — such as obvious mortal damage or decapitation — are clear even to nonmedical people.

Pitfall: no single sign confirms death; in sudden death (hypothermia, poisoning, cardiac arrest) more evidence is needed and resuscitation may be warranted.

retired.text:
When determining a patient's decision-making capacity, consider 8 factors:

{{c1::Impaired intellect (mental limitation or dementia)}}

{{c1::Legal age (18 in most states)}}

{{c1::Alcohol or drug intoxication, or serious injury or illness}}

{{c1::Significant pain}}

{{c1::A significant distracting injury (may mask a more serious one)}}

{{c1::Hearing or visual problems}}

{{c1::A language barrier}}

{{c1::Apparent understanding (asks rational questions)}}
retired.back_extra:
Why: Decision-making capacity is the foundation of consent — an adult who is conscious, rational, and capable of an informed decision may legally refuse care, so these factors decide whose refusal stands.

Cue: Sweep the conversation head to toe — mind, age, chemicals, pain, senses, language, comprehension.

retired.text:
9 scenarios establish medical necessity for ambulance transport:

{{c1::emergency transport when no other means was possible}}

{{c1::restraint needed to prevent injury to self or others}}

{{c1::oxygen or other emergency treatment required during transport}}

{{c1::unconscious or in shock}}

{{c1::signs of acute respiratory or cardiac distress (shortness of breath, chest pain)}}

{{c1::signs suggesting possible acute stroke}}

{{c1::immobility required for an unstabilized or possible fracture}}

{{c1::severe hemorrhage}}

{{c1::bed-confined before and after the trip}}
retired.back_extra:
Why: Medicare and Medicaid reimburse ambulance transport only when documentation shows the trip was medically necessary.

Pitfall: necessity also applies to the level of care — documenting ALS interventions for a patient who did not need them is inappropriate.

HHemorrhage, severe
OOxygen or other emergency treatment during transport
UUnconscious or in shock
SStroke signs
EEmergency — no other means of transport possible
CChest — acute cardiac or respiratory distress
RRestraint needed (injury to self or others)
IImmobility required — unstabilized or possible fracture
BBed-confined before and after

retired.text:
The digestive system, also called the gastrointestinal system, is composed of 10 structures:

{{c1::the gastrointestinal tract (stomach and intestines)}}, {{c1::mouth}}, {{c1::salivary glands}}, {{c1::pharynx}}, {{c1::esophagus}}, {{c1::liver}}, {{c1::gallbladder}}, {{c1::pancreas}}, {{c1::rectum}}, and {{c1::anus}}.
retired.back_extra:
Why: every one of those structures serves a single job, digestion, the processing of food that nourishes the individual cells of the body.

Cue: most of the digestive organs sit inside the abdomen, the second major body cavity, which holds the major organs of digestion and excretion.

retired.text:
Normal systolic blood pressure in mm Hg, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::50 to 70}}

Infant — {{c1::70 to 95}}

Toddler and preschool age — {{c1::80 to 100}}

School age — {{c1::80 to 110}}

Adolescent — {{c1::90 to 110}}

Early, middle, and older adult — {{c1::90 to 130}}
retired.back_extra:
Distinguish: systolic pressure is the only one of the four vital signs that climbs with age — a neonate's floor of 50 mm Hg is little more than half the adult floor of 90.

Pitfall: an adolescent reaches adult pulse and respiratory values but not adult pressure — the systolic ceiling holds at 110 until age 19, then rises to 130.

retired.text:
The nine life-span age groups and the ages each one covers:

Neonate — {{c1::birth to 1 month}}

Infant — {{c1::1 month to 1 year}}

Toddler — {{c1::1 to 3 years}}

Preschool age — {{c1::3 to 6 years}}

School age — {{c1::6 to 12 years}}

Adolescent — {{c1::12 to 18 years}}

Early adult — {{c1::19 to 40 years}}

Middle adult — {{c1::41 to 60 years}}

Older adult — {{c1::61 years and older}}
retired.back_extra:
Why: no other phase of life changes as fast as the first year, which is why those 12 months alone carry two names — neonate for the first month, infant for the remaining eleven.

Pitfall: the childhood bands share a boundary year, so one age can sit in two groups — a 12-year-old is both school age and adolescent — while the adult bands do not overlap, since adolescence ends at 18 and early adulthood starts at 19.

retired.text:
A neonate's body weight follows a predictable course:

At birth: {{c1::6 to 8 lb (3 to 3.5 kg)}}

First week: falls {{c1::5% to 10%}} from fluid loss

Second week onward: gains about {{c1::1 ounce (30 g) per day}}

Doubles birth weight by {{c1::4 to 6 months}}

Triples birth weight by {{c1::1 year}}
retired.back_extra:
Ex: a 7 lb newborn is about 14 lb at 6 months and about 21 lb at 1 year.

Pitfall: doubling and tripling are multiples of the birth weight, not of whatever the infant weighs at the time.

retired.text:
Match each characteristic to the age at which it typically appears in an infant:

Reaches arms out to people; drools → {{c1::4 months}}

Sleeps throughout the night; distinguishes family members from strangers → {{c1::5 months}}

Recognizes familiar faces; uses the eyes to track objects and people → {{c1::2 months}}

Begins teething; sits upright; speaks one-syllable words → {{c1::6 months}}

Brings objects to the mouth; smiles and frowns → {{c1::3 months}}
retired.back_extra:
Distinguish: bringing objects to the mouth is the 3-month characteristic, while deliberately exploring objects by placing them in the mouth comes months later; in the same way, sitting upright at 6 months precedes sitting alone.

Cue: the first half-year develops outward from the eyes, running recognizing and tracking first, then the hands and mouth (reaching, drooling, mouthing), then the trunk and the first one-syllable words.

retired.text:
Match each infant characteristic to the age at which it typically appears:

Pulls self up to stand; explores objects by placing them in the mouth → {{c1::9 months}}

Knows his or her name; walks → {{c1::12 months}}

Afraid of strangers; displays mood swings → {{c1::7 months}}

Begins to walk without assistance; becomes frustrated by restrictions → {{c1::11 months}}

Responds to "no"; can sit alone; plays peek-a-boo → {{c1::8 months}}

Responds to his or her name; crawls efficiently → {{c1::10 months}}
retired.back_extra:
Distinguish: two look-alike pairs split by degree. An infant responds to his or her name at 10 months but knows it at 12, and begins to walk without assistance at 11 months but simply walks at 12.

Cue: the second half-year is one long mobility ladder, sitting alone, then pulling up to stand, then crawling, then walking, and it opens with the social shift at 7 months when the infant first becomes afraid of strangers.

retired.text:
An EMT's radio patient report commonly includes 10 elements, in order:

1. {{c1::Unit ID and service level}}

2. {{c1::Any special alert}}

3. {{c1::Receiving hospital and ETA}}

4. {{c1::Patient's age and sex}}

5. {{c1::Chief complaint and severity}}

6. {{c1::Brief history of current problem}}

7. {{c1::Brief report of physical findings}}

8. {{c1::Summary of care given}}

9. {{c1::Patient's response to treatment}}

10. {{c1::Any additional questions or orders}}
retired.back_extra:
Cue: the report tells the call's story in order — who we are → any alert → where we're headed and when → who the patient is → what's wrong → how it happened → what we found → what we did → how they responded → what else do you need?

Distinguish: element 8 is the care you gave; element 9 is how the patient responded to that care.

Ex: 'Columbus Fire 2-BLS' (element 1); severe trauma → 'trauma alert', heart attack → 'cardiac alert' (element 2); physical findings cover level of consciousness, general appearance, pertinent abnormalities, and vital signs (element 7).
